sources.citation: KAKEN project pages 26370475 (Kobayashi, 'Complexification in the South Asian languages in hill areas', 2014-2017) and 18H00672 (Osada/Kobayashi/Badenoch, 'Documentation of endangered languages in Munda', 2018-2022), NII.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; final report of 18H00672 states Kobayashi 'has almost finished writing a grammar of Korwa. We have a plan to publish it near future'; outputs listed are the three eTULIP folk-tale texts and a 2017 talk 'The past suffixes of Hill Korwa'. Kobayashi's researchmap list (to 2025) shows no published Korwa grammar yet.

sources.note: Nothing. The Korwa sketch has only a 'Pronunciation' paragraph (palatal nasal retention, v ~ l correspondence, semi-consonants inconsistently marked); unlike the Santali (p. ~41 'Accent.—In words of two syllables the accent usually rests on the first..') and Mundari (p. 85 'The accent is the same as in Santali') sections, there is no 'Accent' paragraph for Korwa.

tone.quote: There is no phonemic length contrast, as we will discuss below. [...] the vowel in the pre-suffix syllable is often lengthened and receives stress realized as a falling tone, e.g., tula ‘to make’, tuˈlā-ter-a PST-FIN; tora ‘to go away’, toˈrā-ku ‘they went’; ara ‘son-in-law’, aˈrā-laŋ 1DU.IN ‘our son-in-law’; oŋgol ‘to think’, oŋgˈl-ē-tan OBJ-NPT; ɲel ‘to look’, ˈɲēl-a FIN. This lengthening tends to apply to a vowel in the initial or peninitial syllable. [fn. 4:] According to Barker (1953: 32), the vowel length is a concomitant feature of stress, which differs depending on tempo and focus, e.g., normal /ˈsabɛme/ ‘catch him!’ vs. emphatic speech /saˈbeːme/ ‘catch HIM!’
tone.locator: p. 7 §1 (no length contrast); p. 8 Ch. 1 §1(b) 'Vowels with Lengthening and Falling Tones' and fn. 4; cf. §3(a) p. 11 (schwa in unstressed syllables, after Barker 1953: 33), §11 p. ~19 (postpositions 'form their own stress domains'), §53(b) p. 51 (question particle ja 'with rising tone' = intonation)
tone.summary: No tone system: Hill Korwa is described with a segment-only inventory; falling pitch is the realization of (length-cued) stress on the pre-suffixal/base-final syllable, and rising pitch is question intonation.

sources.note: The only dedicated first-hand phonology of Korwa (1950s fieldwork). Secondhand: 'According to Barker (1953: 32), the vowel length is a concomitant feature of stress, which differs depending on tempo and focus' (Kobayashi 2025: 8 fn. 4); Barker treats [ə] as a phoneme of unstressed open syllables (ibid. p. 11); Horo & Anderson 2021 Table 2 summarize it as prominence on the 'Second/last syllable of stem (Barker 1953)', cue 'Duration?'. Nothing in any citation suggests Barker posited tone; expected to contain an explicit suprasegmental/stress section and possibly an explicit no-tone remark.
